body.statement: Always \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm{com}}\subseteq\mathcal I_{\mathrm{sep}}\), where \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm{sep}}\) is the internal outer relaxation that permits the two arms to use different posterior pairs and is not a published marginal-sensitivity procedure.  For the observed law and budgets in \(P^\star\), the worked exact certificate \(\mathcal C^\star\) gives \(L\in[-107500302/10^9,-107500301/10^9]\), \(L_{\mathrm{sep}}=-3461701/31346200\in[-110434471/10^9,-110434470/10^9]\), \(R\in[539509967/10^9,539509968/10^9]\), and \(R_{\mathrm{sep}}=84380923/150997400\in[558823681/10^9,558823682/10^9]\).  Thus both endpoint inequalities are strict, and they remain strict on a relatively open neighborhood of the displayed interior observed law and finite budgets.  The attaining witness itself has \(r_1=53/100\), \(r_0=6/25\), \(\operatorname{OR}(A,U)=16\), \(\theta_1=247/7<36\), \(\theta_0=36\), \(\tau(P^\star)=-1/10\), and nominal contrast \(r_1-r_0=29/100\).
body.justification: The strict open-set gap demonstrates that common-law compatibility has empirical content beyond a hand-picked numerical coincidence.
body.gap: The internal armwise relaxation removes only common-posterior compatibility inside the present model.  Dorn--Guo's marginal sensitivity model is generally non-nested and informs the sharpness strategy; no published result isolates this shared-binary-posterior loss under simultaneous treatment and outcome odds budgets.
body.consumer: Analysts avoid reporting materially overwide intervals that combine mutually incompatible armwise confounder distributions.
body.proof_tex:
For a stratum \(x\), abbreviate a posterior pair by \(d\in D_{A,x}\).  For every such \(d\),
\[
q^-_{1,x}(d)-q^+_{0,x}(d)
\geq \min_{e\in D_{A,x}}q^-_{1,x}(e)
-\max_{f\in D_{A,x}}q^+_{0,x}(f).
\tag{16}
\]
Taking the minimum of the left side over \(d\), multiplying by \(\lambda_x>0\), and summing proves \(L\geq L_{\mathrm{sep}}\).  Similarly,
\[
q^+_{1,x}(d)-q^-_{0,x}(d)
\leq \max_{e\in D_{A,x}}q^+_{1,x}(e)
-\min_{f\in D_{A,x}}q^-_{0,x}(f),
\tag{17}
\]
so \(R\leq R_{\mathrm{sep}}\).  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}envelope}\) identifies the common-pair interval, while Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}separate\text{-}pair\text{-}relaxation}\) defines the armwise outer relaxation.  Equations (16)--(17) therefore give
\[
L_{\mathrm{sep}}\leq L\leq R\leq R_{\mathrm{sep}},
\qquad
\mathcal I_{\mathrm{com}}\subseteq\mathcal I_{\mathrm{sep}}.
\tag{18}
\]

We next verify that the law named in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}rational\text{-}witness}\) is feasible.  Its marginal confounder prevalence and treatment odds ratio are
\[
\pi=\frac12\frac45+\frac12\frac15=\frac12,
\qquad
\operatorname{OR}\left(\frac45,\frac15\right)
=\frac{(4/5)(4/5)}{(1/5)(1/5)}=16.
\tag{19}
\]
The two observed arm risks and outcome odds ratios are
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_1&=\frac45\frac{13}{20}+\frac15\frac1{20}=\frac{53}{100},
&\theta_1&=\frac{(13/20)(19/20)}{(1/20)(7/20)}=\frac{247}{7}<36,\\
r_0&=\frac15\frac45+\frac45\frac1{10}=\frac6{25},
&\theta_0&=\frac{(4/5)(9/10)}{(1/10)(1/5)}=36.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
\]
Bayes' rule gives \(P^\star(A=1\mid U=1)=4/5\) and \(P^\star(A=1\mid U=0)=1/5\).  These probabilities and every displayed outcome risk lie strictly between zero and one.  Drawing the two potential outcomes independently conditional on \(U\), as specified in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}rational\text{-}witness}\), makes every full-data cell positive and gives \((Y(0),Y(1))\perp A\mid U\).  Equations (19)--(20) verify all sensitivity inequalities.  Thus \(P^\star\in\mathcal M^\circ\), and
\[
\tau(P^\star)
=\frac12\left(\frac{13}{20}+\frac1{20}-\frac45-\frac1{10}\right)
=-\frac1{10},
\qquad
r_1-r_0=\frac{29}{100}.
\tag{21}
\]

It remains to validate the exact endpoint transcript rather than taking its construction as proof.  On the reverse arc in (C8), \(w_0=W(t)>t=w_1\), and
\[
w_0(1-w_1)=16w_1(1-w_0),
\qquad
16w_0(1-w_1)-w_1(1-w_0)=255w_1(1-w_0)>0.
\tag{22}
\]
Since \(p=1/2\), \(\pi-w_1=(W-t)/2>0\) and \(\pi-w_0=(t-W)/2<0\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}outcome\text{-}budget\text{-}extrema}\) therefore makes the common lower branch \(J_{1/36}\) and the common upper branch \(J_{36}\), exactly as recorded in (C1)--(C2).

We first rule out missing interior extrema without appealing to numerical branch persistence.  For fixed \(r\in(0,1)\) and \(\vartheta>0\), let \(z(w)\) be the feasible mixture root, \(f(z)=\vartheta z/\{1+(\vartheta-1)z\}\), and \(\delta(w)=f\{z(w)\}-z(w)\).  Differentiating \(r=z+w\delta\), which is legal because
\[
D(w)=1-w+wf'\{z(w)\}>0,
\]
gives
\[
z'(w)=-\frac{\delta(w)}{D(w)},
\qquad
\delta(w)+w\delta'(w)=\frac{\delta(w)}{D(w)},
\qquad
\delta(w)-(1-w)\delta'(w)=\frac{\delta(w)f'\{z(w)\}}{D(w)}.
\tag{23}
\]
If \(\vartheta>1\), then \(\delta>0\), so (23) implies
\[
-\frac{\delta(w)}{w}<\delta'(w)<\frac{\delta(w)}{1-w}
\qquad(0<w<1).
\tag{24}
\]
On \(\mathcal I_R\), put \(e=w_0-w_1>0\) and \(S=\delta_1(w_1)+\delta_0(w_0)>0\).  The upper common objective is \(29/100+eS/2\).  By (24), \(e<w_0\) and \(e<1-w_1\) imply
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial w_0}\left(\frac{eS}{2}\right)
=\frac{S+e\delta_0'(w_0)}2>\frac{\delta_1(w_1)}2>0,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial w_1}\left(\frac{eS}{2}\right)
=\frac{-S+e\delta_1'(w_1)}2<-\frac{\delta_0(w_0)}2<0.
\tag{25}
\]
Thus there is no interior stationary point.  For \(0<\vartheta<1\), apply the same argument to \(-\delta>0\); the lower objective strictly decreases as the posterior separation is enlarged and again has no interior stationary point.  Complementing \(U\) proves the same facts on \(\mathcal I_F\).  The separate objectives are even simpler: on \(\mathcal I_R\), their derivatives in the opposite arm's posterior coordinate are the nonzero quantities \(\pm\delta_a/2\).  Hence their relevant extrema also lie on the two arcs, diagonal, or corners.  This proves that (C8) is not merely a listed set of cells but an exhaustive candidate reduction.

For the remaining one-dimensional candidates, (C2) is the implicit-differentiation numerator obtained from the two mixture equations; (23) shows that the factors \(\partial F_a/\partial z_a\) cannot vanish at a feasible root.  The resultant identity defining (C3)--(C4) therefore shows that every legal arc stationary point has \(g_-(t)=0\) or \(g_+(t)=0\).  The deterministic Sturm recurrence stated before (C5), together with the variation differences \(8-6=2\), proves that each polynomial has exactly two roots in \((0,1)\).  The four one-unit variation drops in (C5) isolate all four roots.  Substitution into the original systems, the nonzero Jacobian enclosures (C7), the legal-risk checks following (C7), and interval Newton contraction validate one and only one legal stationary triple in each box.  Thus no resultant root is missed, duplicated, or admitted through a cleared denominator.

The diagonal and corner objective is exactly \(29/100\).  Comparing this value and all four enclosures in (C6) proves
\[
L\in[-107500302/10^9,-107500301/10^9],
\qquad
R\in[539509967/10^9,539509968/10^9].
\tag{26}
\]
Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}complete\text{-}semialgebraic\text{-}certificate}\) justifies the exact resultant, Sturm, saturation, and interval-Newton operations used by this fixed-input transcript; the preceding cell argument and the complete coefficients and sign data in \(\mathcal C^\star\) supply its independently checkable input and output.

For the separate extrema, (C9) is obtained by the same exact implicit differentiation and elimination.  The sole additional resultant root lying in \((0,1)\), \(t=9/325\), forces \(z_0=414/395>1\) and is therefore rejected by Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\); all remaining extra factors have roots outside \((0,1)\).  Direct rational substitution of the four legal records in (C10), followed by comparison with the endpoint values in the certificate, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{\mathrm{sep}}
&=\frac{94711}{277400}-\frac{2553}{5650}
=-\frac{3461701}{31346200}
\in[-110434471/10^9,-110434470/10^9],\\
R_{\mathrm{sep}}
&=\frac{212689}{302600}-\frac{1797}{12475}
=\frac{84380923}{150997400}
\in[558823681/10^9,558823682/10^9].
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}
\]
Exact interval subtraction of (26)--(27) yields
\[
L-L_{\mathrm{sep}}
\in[2934168/10^9,2934170/10^9],
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{sep}}-R
\in[19313713/10^9,19313715/10^9].
\tag{28}
\]
Both inclusions in (18) are consequently strict at the witness.

Finally we prove open-set strictness from value-function continuity, without assuming persistence of any active algebraic branch.  Let \(\gamma\) vary near \(16\).  For an interior pair write \(s_a=\operatorname{logit}(w_a)\).  The exposure region is \(|s_1-s_0|\leq\log\gamma\).  Given \(\gamma_n\to\gamma\) and a pair in \(D_\gamma\), keep \((s_0+s_1)/2\) fixed and truncate \(s_1-s_0\) to \([-\log\gamma_n,\log\gamma_n]\); the inverse-logit pairs then lie in \(D_{\gamma_n}\) and converge to the original pair.  The two constant corners belong to every \(D_\gamma\).  Conversely, every limit of \(d_n\in D_{\gamma_n}\) satisfies the two weak polynomial inequalities for \(D_\gamma\).  Hence
\[
d_H(D_{\gamma_n},D_\gamma)\longrightarrow0,
\tag{29}
\]
where \(d_H\) is Hausdorff distance on the compact square.

Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\) and Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}closed\text{-}chart\text{-}extension}\) make every endpoint objective jointly continuous in \((p,r_0,r_1,\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1,d)\) near the witness; reciprocal budgets are continuous because all budgets remain positive.  To see continuity of a minimum directly, choose minimizers \(d_n\in D_{\gamma_n}\).  Compactness gives a convergent subsequence, (29) places its limit in \(D_\gamma\), and joint continuity gives the lower limit inequality.  Approximating any minimizer in \(D_\gamma\) by pairs in \(D_{\gamma_n}\), again using (29), gives the upper limit inequality.  Maxima follow by negating the objective.  The same argument applies separately to the four armwise extrema.  Thus \(L-L_{\mathrm{sep}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{sep}}-R\) are continuous functions of the interior observed summaries and finite budgets at the witness.  Their strictly positive lower bounds in (28) remain positive on a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood.  This proves the asserted stable strict tightening.
